Q: Validate firewalld config with ansible A:

You were asking about /etc/firewalld/firewalld.conf. I don't know of a way to pre-validate that. May I suggest using lineinfile instead of a template? It tends to be less risky because it leaves the structure of the file intact.

This answer applies to a related task for the benefit of people finding this via Google, as I did: pre-validating firewalld XML files.

You can use xmllint to validate the XML files.

Here is the step-by-step:

  • Get the XML schema files. They may already exist, probably in /usr/share/firewalld and named something like zone.rng or zone.xsd, or they may be missing.

If they are missing:

  • Download them from https://github.com/firewalld/firewalld/tree/main/config/xmlschema (keep in mind that this schema could have changed compared to your version).

  • Place them in a directory under Ansibles files directory, succh as files/xmlschema

  • Use Ansible to copy the XML schemas to the host:

- name: Install firewalld XML schema
  ansible.builtin.copy:
    src: xmlschema/
    dest: /opt/firewall_schemas/
  • Run xmllint to do the validation. Add this to your template or copy task:
validate: xmllint --noout --schema /opt/firewall_schemas/zone.xsd %s`

Obviously, change the path to the schema as needed.

Disclaimer: this answer was written and tested by a human, but I used Google Gemini to develop the concept.

Q: Replacing movemem() with inline assembly for vga graphics A:

Are SEG_buffer, OFF_buffer, SEG_vga, OFF_vga, and SIZE variables or are they just immediates?

If these are memory-based variables, then havoc is what you'd get because of the order of the assembly operations. Once mov ds, ax has done its job, the remaining fetches will come from the wrong segment. Just load DS last. (In movedata(SEG_buffer, OFF_buffer, SEG_vga, OFF_vga, SIZE);, it is Turbo C that will do the de-referencing.)
If these identifiers are indeed just immediates, then TASM would have to reject mov ds, SEG_buffer, but if they are variables then the direct loading of a segment register has always been possible!

Surely this is the legacy video mode 13h for the VGA 320x200 256-color resolution. Where else could you meaningfully write 64000 bytes in one chunk. The question then arises why there are so many arguments to this operation? The video aperture is fixed at ES:DI=A000:0000, the length is fixed at CX=64000, and your private buffer at 64000 bytes will occupy its very own memory segment and so an offset SI=0 is to be expected.

push ds
push es
push cx
push si
push di
mov  cx, 0A000h
mov  es, cx
xor  di, di
mov  ds, SEG_buffer   ; (*)
xor  si, si
mov  cx, 64000/2
rep  movsw            ; (**)
pop  di
pop  si
pop  cx
pop  es
pop  ds

(*) Being a variable is what makes the most sense. Normally, you don't know where your application got loaded and therefore you'd have calculated the location of your private buffer and stored the result in a memory-based variable.
(**) You can trust Turbo C that the direction flag will be clear already.
